title: 3-Read Friday #112: Non-examples, screen time, and better evidence for teachers
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton's weekly digest curates three items for educators, and this issue leans on the linked source pieces for its depth. Jamie Clark's DistillED post explores non-examples: deliberately chosen contrast cases that share surface features with a concept but lack its critical defining feature, illustrated through a Year 8 English class that over-generalized 'pathetic fallacy' to any mention of weather until a non-example drew the boundary. Dan Meyer's Math Worlds essay challenges blunt calls to reduce screen time, arguing that classrooms need a richer 'melody' of resources rather than either constant screens or none at all, since a lesson built entirely around solo device work is as monotonous as one built entirely around teacher lecture. Jim Hewitt and Nidhi Sachdeva's Evidence Checker gives teachers direct access to research so they can evaluate classroom claims themselves. Barton frames all three as contributions to the same project: building clearer, more disciplined, more evidence-grounded teaching practice.
points: Plan non-examples in advance rather than improvising them: Clark's framework requires they be closely related to the concept, sharing surface features but lacking the one critical defining feature, so students learn the boundary and not just the label.

Meyer's melody metaphor reframes the screen-time debate: the problem isn't screens as an instrument but a monotonous composition — a lesson is as dull when it's all device time as when it's all teacher lecture, so the fix is variety of resources, not blanket bans.
Give teachers direct access to evidence via tools like The Evidence Checker rather than filtering all research through intermediaries who may simplify, reframe, or oversell findings.

Clark's Year 8 pathetic-fallacy example shows the cost of skipping non-examples: without a boundary case, students generalized the term to any weather reference in any text, including a phone weather forecast.

Distinguish strong from weak evidence when evaluating classroom claims — AI-powered research tools can help teachers ask deeper follow-up questions about methodology and effect size rather than accepting a headline finding at face value.
quotes: A non-example is a deliberately chosen contrast case — an instance that almost fits a concept but doesn't, because it's missing the critical defining feature. The aim of a non-example is to draw a sharp boundary around what a concept actually is.

An English teacher introduces pathetic fallacy in a Year 8 unit on Gothic fiction. The examples are well chosen — a storm breaks as the protagonist discovers the body, fog descends as the detective loses the trail, rain hammers the windows during the argument.

In their essays, students begin identifying every weather reference in every text as pathetic fallacy. One student argues that a weather forecast on a character's phone is pathetic fallacy because it predicts a storm.

Teaching is the work of composition. Teachers compose the resources in a classroom—including education technology, but also paper, textbooks, questions, explanations, whiteboards, other students, the physical space, etc.—into experiences that help students learn.
These devices are some of humanity's most incredible achievements, but when students use them in schools they often hear only two notes—teacher explanation and screens.

Nuance" is an overused word to describe someone's views... but I don't know of a better one to describe Dan's writing on Edtech. Here, he argues that the call to ban (or reduce) screens in schools is too blunt.

I love research. I love AI. Therefore, I love this. A new AI-powered tool, The Evidence Checker, gives teachers direct and nuanced (there we go again!) access to educational research so they can evaluate classroom claims for themselves rather than relying on intermediaries.
